extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties participating in PTAB trial proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, and their counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and prosecuting petitions and responses in PTAB trial proceedings (IPR, PGR, CBM, DER), covering substantive, procedural, and formal requirements the Board applies when deciding institution and early motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition specificity requirement (identify claims, grounds, evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 312(a)(3)/322(a)(3) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.22(a)(2)/42.204(b)(4), the petition must identify in writing and with particularity each claim challenged, the grounds for the challenge to each claim, and the evidence supporting the grounds; where grounds are based on prior art, the petition must specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where a party fails to state relevance or to identify specific portions of evidence supporting the challenge (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104(b)(5), 42.204(b)(5)). Provide a full statement of the reasons for relief requested, including detailed explanation of the significance of the evidence, material facts, and governing law, rules, and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid facially duplicative (redundant) grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will not consider multiple grounds that are facially duplicative or presented in a redundant manner (CBM2012-00003, notice 7); petitioner may be required to elect non-redundant grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple grounds are redundant, the Board may grant a short cure period for the petitioner to select non-redundant grounds and state that grounds not selected will not be considered. Petitioners should expressly identify how each ground differs (e.g., alternative claim constructions or facts) to avoid redundancy elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizontal redundancy — multiple references as interchangeable alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Horizontal redundancy occurs when a plurality of prior art references are presented as distinct alternatives that each provide essentially the same teaching for the same claim limitation without explaining why one reference better satisfies the limitation than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If references are not identical, the petition must explain why each reference is preferable in some respect; otherwise the references will be collectively viewed as horizontally redundant and not entitled to consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical redundancy — partial vs full combination redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertical redundancy arises when petitioner asserts both that a subset of references (partial combination) and the entire combination render a claim obvious without explaining when the subset is the stronger assertion versus the full combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner must provide a bi-directional explanation showing why reliance in part may be stronger in some instances and reliance in whole stronger in others; absent such explanation, the assertions are vertically redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must state differences between claimed invention and prior art for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: For obviousness grounds, petitioner must expressly state the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art relied upon; the Board will not infer those differences from other parts of the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petition that fails to identify the differences risks denial of the corresponding obviousness ground for failing to adequately state a claim for relief (Graham v. John Deere principle applied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thresholds for institution and ultimate burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Institution thresholds differ by proceeding: CBM and PGR require 'more likely than not' that petitioner will prevail (35 U.S.C. 324(a)); IPR requires a 'reasonable likelihood' (35 U.S.C. 314(a)). The ultimate burden to prove a proposition at trial is 'preponderance of the evidence' (35 U.S.C. 316(e); 326(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions should be drafted to meet the applicable institution standard and to present pretrial evidence sufficient to support a preponderance showing if trial is instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board will resolve vagueness and ambiguity against petitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: In evaluating petitions the Board will address only the basis, rationale, and reasoning put forth by the petitioner and will resolve vagueness and ambiguity in the petition against the petitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague or ambiguous explanations of how references are combined or how claim elements map to prior art; unclear reasoning will result in denial of grounds prior to institution (see CBM2012-00003, notice 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board may deny grounds prior to institution (42.208(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 42.208(b) the Board may deny some or all grounds for unpatentability at any time prior to institution of post-grant review; denial of a ground is a Board decision not to institute review on that ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners should not assume grounds survive to institution; substantive review can occur before preliminary responses are filed and can narrow issues or deny grounds early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to enlarge petition page limits (interests of justice standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)(2) allows motions to waive petition page limits, but petitioner must show in the motion how a waiver is 'in the interests of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To succeed, petitioner must meaningfully explain why limitations of the challenged claims could not be addressed within the standard page limit (e.g., why claim complexity requires more pages), show that additional references are not cumulative, and provide concrete examples of content that cannot fit within the page limit. Historically, such motions are rarely granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical considerations re enlarged petitions and estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing an enlarged petition (and having the motion to admit it denied) may affect estoppel: for IPRs/PGRs, a ground that could not 'reasonably' have been raised may avoid estoppel (35 U.S.C. 315(e), 325(e)); CBM estoppel is limited to any ground the petitioner raised during the proceeding, so filing an enlarged CBM petition carries risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether submitting an enlarged petition could preserve grounds from estoppel (IPR/PGR) versus creating exposure to CBM estoppel; weigh risks before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory notices and counsel identification timing
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.8(b) requires that the patent owner or applicant respondent in a DER identify lead and backup counsel within 21 days of service of the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply promptly with mandatory notice requirements to avoid procedural issues; where parties are searching for counsel, the Board has granted short extensions in discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro hac vice admission requirements and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 42.10(c) and Board orders, the Board may recognize counsel pro hac vice upon a showing of good cause, subject to lead counsel being a registered practitioner and other conditions; motions for pro hac vice are authorized no sooner than 21 days after service of the petition, oppositions must be filed within one week of the motion, and no reply is authorized unless the Board permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pro hac vice motion must contain a statement of facts showing good cause and be accompanied by an affidavit/declaration by the individual attesting to specified factors (bar membership in good standing, no suspensions/disbarments, no denied applications, no sanctions, will comply with Practice Guide and Part 42, subject to USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility, list of other pro hac vice appearances in last 3 years, and familiarity with subject matter). Explain any negative facts fully. Behavior in related litigation (e.g., protective order violations) can defeat a pro hac vice motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order and sealing practices (motion to seal)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.54(a) permits motions to seal where the motion includes a proposed protective order (standing protective order is provided in the Office Patent Trial Practice Guide) and a certification that the moving party conferred in good faith with affected parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standing protective order is normally entered automatically upon filing a petition or institution of derivation; parties may file stipulated protective orders with added safeguards (e.g., prosecution bar). Information remains sealed only until 45 days after denial of a petition to institute or 45 days after final judgment in a trial — timely motions to expunge are necessary to preserve confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary response evidence limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.107(c) and 42.207(c), the preliminary response shall not present new testimonial evidence beyond that already of record, except as authorized by the Board; 42.65(a) bars testimony on U.S. patent law or patent examination practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New testimonial evidence in a preliminary response is allowed only in 'the interests of justice' (e.g., evidence going to standing). Requests to introduce testimony for credibility attacks or routine technical disputes are routinely denied and are better reserved for trial if instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page limit for patent owner preliminary response
rubrics_metrics.description: The page limits for a patent owner preliminary response are the same as the page limits for the petition (Rule 42.24(b)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page limit is determined by the number of pages authorized for the petition type, not by the actual number of pages the petitioner filed; plan preliminary responses accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions practice — prior authorization required
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 37 C.F.R. § 42.29(b) states that a motion will not be entered without Board authorization; authorization may be provided generally or during the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized motions (and oppositions to unauthorized motions) may be expunged. When in doubt about procedural filings, contact the Board for authorization/guidance rather than filing unauthorized pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing accuracy and ministerial care
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministerial acts of filing documents in Board proceedings are critically important; clerical errors (e.g., filing a motion in the wrong proceeding) can result in expungement and wasted effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the same level of care for filing and docketing as for substantive drafting; if a procedural problem arises, contact the Board and request guidance or a conference call per the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and spacing requirements to enforce page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(2)(iii) requires double spacing generally (except claim charts, headings, tables of contents/authorities, indices, signature blocks, and certificates of service) and the Office notes parties should not use line spacing, font size, or margins to evade page limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place substantive argument or claim construction into claim charts to evade double-spacing requirements; paralegals and the Board monitor improper usage and may require correction or reject attempts to circumvent page limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim chart usage and single-spacing exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim charts may be single spaced and may be used to provide the element-by-element showing of where claim elements are found in prior art (per 37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(2)(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim charts should be limited to the permitted element-by-element showings; placing full argumentative text in claim charts to avoid double-spacing is improper and may be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margin and orientation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(2)(iv) requires margins of at least 2.5 centimeters (1 inch) on all sides; the Board has expressed displeasure with landscape-oriented claim charts though no explicit prohibition exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure margins meet rule requirements; if using landscape claim charts for readability, consider conferring with the Board because enforcement practices may change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit filing and numbering requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.63(a) requires all evidence be filed as exhibits; § 42.63(c) requires each party's exhibits to be uniquely numbered sequentially in a Board-specified range (petitioner 1001–1999; patent owner 2001–2999); § 42.63(d) prescribes exhibit format and marking requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-sequential or improperly numbered exhibits are common defects that typically trigger five-business-day cure notices and can require renumbering of the petition, declarations, and all citations — plan exhibit numbering carefully to avoid heavy corrective work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal defect cure periods and non-curable defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal defects in petitions typically result in short cure deadlines (commonly five business days), but some defects may be non-curable or extremely burdensome to cure (e.g., exhibit renumbering that affects multiple documents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and avoid common formal defects (formatting, margins, spacing, exhibit numbering) because cure may be impractical or insufficient to remedy rule non-compliance; assure initial filings conform strictly to Part 42 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary relief and where to raise standing challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing challenges and attacks on a petition are properly raised in the patent owner preliminary response rather than by separate pre-institution motions (e.g., requests to file separate motions were denied where the preliminary response was the appropriate vehicle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the preliminary response to raise challenges to petitioner standing or other attacks on the petition; do not expect separate unauthorized motions to be accepted by the Board for issues that belong in the preliminary response.
